newsitem.title: INDONESIA: ASEAN asked to focus on investment, not trade.
newsitem.headline: ASEAN asked to focus on investment, not trade.

text.p: A two-day meeting focusing on business opportunities in Southeast Asia ended on Thursday with calls by the U.S. delegation for more investment.

George David, chief executive officer of United Technologies Corp and leader of the U.S. delegation to the first ASEAN Business Summit, said the region's growth was trade-driven but more investment was needed to sustain development.
"Foreign direct investment in many ASEAN nations is a little lower than many economists believe it should be," he told reporters.
"These economies are import and export-driven and they would be stronger economies with higher foreign direct investment, especially in the manufacturing and technology sectors."

ASEAN -- the Association of South East Asian nations -- groups Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, the Philippines, Vietnam and Brunei. Cambodia, Laos and Burma are expected to join the bloc later this year.

Participants at the summit have said that with the adoption of an ASEAN Free Trade Area (AFTA) by 2003, the first step toward a borderless economy, and the liberalisation of trade between Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) countries by 2020, the region should record explosive growth in the early part of the 21st century.
They said Southeast Asia should have one billion consumers and $2.0 trillion in combined gross domestic product by 2020, up from the current 400 million and $600 billion respectively.
Some 600 business leaders from 30 countries, including about 200 from the United States, attended the meeting.
ASEAN secretary-general Ajit Singh said regional businessmen needed to ensure they were not slow in taking advantage of the liberalisation efforts.
"It would be ironic if foreign businessmen seize the initiative and derive greater advantages from AFTA rather than our own businessmen," he said.
However, one senior ASEAN businessman said governments needed to do more.
Aburizal Bakrie, president of the ASEAN Chambers of Commerce and Industry, told reporters that AFTA's target date of 2003 was distant.

"My question is are we going to wait until 2003? Are we going to do it (integrate the private sector) now? If we are going to do it now, we need some cooperation from the governments," he said. "They should lower their tariffs."

Bakrie was responding to suggestions by Malaysian Trade Minister Rafidah Aziz on Wednesday that the private sector in the region set up ASEAN conglomerates that could take advantage of complementary businesses tapping the global economy.
"The ASEAN market should be opened at least for the projects which are already under AICO (the ASEAN Industrial Cooperation scheme)," he said.

AICO is a fast-track version of the AFTA proposals to reduce tariffs to between 0-5 percent by 2003, under which companies from two ASEAN countries can apply for reduced tariffs for products manufactured by a joint venture.
But the reduced tariffs will apply only to the two countries concerned, and Bakrie said AICO should be expanded to all ASEAN nations for non-sensitive products.
